facts.statement: In 1998, researchers Ji Shuan and Luis Chiappe identified a specimen of Confuciusornis that appeared distinct from others in the National Geological Museum of China.
facts.quote: In 1998 Ji Shuan and Luis Chiappe discovered among the many specimens of the National Geological Museum of China at Beijing assigned to Confuciusornis, an exemplar that seemed somewhat different.

facts.statement: In 1999, Ji, Chiappe, and Ji Qiang formally named the species Changchengornis hengdaoziensis.
facts.quote: In 1999 Ji, Chiappe and Ji Qiang named the type species and only species of Changchengornis: Changchengornis hengdaoziensis.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen GMV-2129 was discovered near the village of Jianshangou in Liaoning province within the Jianshangou Beds of the Hengdaozi Member.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, GMV-2129, was found near the village of Jianshangou in Liaoning province, in the Jianshangou Beds of the Hengdaozi Member of the Yixian Formation

facts.statement: The holotype consists of a largely complete, articulated, but compressed and damaged skeleton preserved as a plate and counterplate.
facts.quote: It consists of a plate and counterplate, GMV-2129a/b, showing a largely complete and articulated but compressed and somewhat damaged skeleton.

facts.statement: Much of the feathering on the holotype specimen is preserved in an excellent state.
facts.quote: Much of the feathering has been preserved in an excellent state of preservation.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Changchengornis is smaller than the smallest known specimens of its relative Confuciusornis.
facts.quote: The type specimen is rather small, smaller than the smallest known specimens of Confuciusornis.

facts.statement: The deltopectoral crest of the humerus in Changchengornis is not pierced.
facts.quote: The deltopectoral crest of the humerus is not pierced.

facts.statement: The holotype GMV-2129 displays two elongated, ribbon-like tail feathers similar to those found in male Confuciusornis specimens.
facts.quote: GMV-2129 also shows two elongated, ribbon-like tail feathers as found in some specimens of Confuciusornis, that are often considered to be the males.

facts.statement: The fossil suggests the presence of a head tuft or crest that would resemble modern turacos, though this feature might be an artifact of conservation.
facts.quote: Also, the fossil gives the impression of a head tuft or crest being present; if so, the outline of its head must have borne an uncanny resemblance to today's Tauraco or turacos in general but it could also be an artefact of conservation.

facts.statement: Remains of Changchengornis have been found in the Chaomidianzi Formation in China, dating to the Barremian-Aptian boundary approximately 125 million years ago.
facts.quote: Its remains have been found in the People's Republic of China, in Chaomidianzi Formation rocks from around the Barremian-Aptian boundary, deposited 125 million years ago.

facts.statement: In 1999, Changchengornis was assigned to the family Confuciusornithidae.
facts.quote: In 1999 it was assigned to the Confuciusornithidae.

facts.statement: The time range for Changchengornis is the Barremian to Aptian, spanning from 125.77 to 119.57 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Aptian (125.77 to 119.57 million years ago)

rejected.quote: Compared to the latter, Changchengornis had a beak that was more pointed, slightly hooked at the tip, proportionally shorter, and higher at the back.
